subject: ENGLISH LANGUAGE
title: Reading: Intensive Reading (Digital Texts)
overview: Digital texts are poems, stories and pictures you read on a screen. In this sub-strand you will read an original narrative of about 320 words and a poem about a favourite game, answer questions, and learn how to find safe, suitable information online. You will also turn ideas into a simple mind map and a crossword.

lessons.title: Reading a digital narrative
objectives: Read a narrative of about 320 words and follow the events.
Work out the meaning of words from the story.
lessons.intro: A story on a tablet still needs a careful reader. The pictures may move, but the meaning sits in the words. Read this narrative as if it were on a screen, and pause when a sentence tells you how a character feels.
lessons.notes:
### How to read a digital story
Read the title first. Then read each paragraph before you tap ahead. If the story is animated, watch the picture and read the words together. The picture can show a feeling, but the words tell you what happened.

If you meet a new word, read the sentence again. A word's neighbours often give you its meaning.

### One Goal More
The sun was already warm when our class walked to the field for the netball match. I carried the ball. My friend carried a spare whistle for the referee, our games captain. We wore the school kit, blue shirts and white shorts. The other team wore green.

Before the game our coach spoke quietly. She told us to listen for the whistle, to pass quickly and not to try to score alone. A loud voice was not enough, she said. Our faces and our hands had to help our teammates. She smiled and gave a thumbs-up. We were nervous, but we were ready.

The referee blew the whistle. I ran towards the centre. The first pass came to me, but I held it too long and the other team took the ball. They scored. Our crowd grew quiet. I looked at the coach. She did not frown. She pointed to her ear, which meant listen, then pointed to a teammate who was free. I nodded and jogged back into place.

In the second half I remembered her gesture. I did not hug the ball. I threw it to the player nearest the goal. She caught it, aimed carefully and scored. The score was level. We shouted with joy, and we also clapped when the other captain made a fine catch. Fair play is part of any game we love.

Near the end the ball slipped from my hands. I felt cross with myself. A teammate touched my shoulder and told me to try again. I took a breath, received the next pass and scored. The final whistle blew. We had won by one goal.

We shook hands with the other team. The coach said we had listened, passed and not given up, and that this is how a team wins. I walked away with dusty shoes and a light heart. My favourite game had taught me more than how to score.

### After reading
This story has about 320 words. Retell it in four steps: before the match, the first goal against us, the equaliser, and the winning goal. Then ask what the story teaches. The writer learns that passing, listening and fair play matter as much as scoring.

keyWords.meaning: a story that tells events in order
a movement, such as pointing, that sends a message
playing by the rules and showing respect to the other team
equal, as when both teams have the same score

examples.problem: Factual: Why did the other team score the first goal?
steps: Find the paragraph that begins with the whistle.
Look at what the narrator did with the first pass.
examples.answer: The narrator held the ball too long, and the other team took it.

examples.problem: Inferential: Why does the narrator say the game taught more than how to score?
steps: Look at the coach's last comment and the handshake.
The lesson is about how the team behaved, not only the result.
examples.answer: Because listening, passing, trying again and fair play mattered as much as the winning goal.

activity.title: Read the story together
materials: The story One Goal More on paper or on a shared screen
steps: Read the story silently once.
In pairs, read it aloud, changing your voice when the narrator is nervous, cross or glad.
Underline two words whose meaning you can guess from the sentences around them, and write those meanings.
Answer the practice questions, then check them against the story.

practice.question: What colours did the two teams wear?
practice.answer: The narrator's team wore blue shirts and white shorts. The other team wore green.

practice.question: What did the coach's point to her ear mean?
What does level mean when the story says the score was level?
practice.answer: Both teams had the same score.

practice.question: What did the teams do after the final whistle?

summary: Read a digital story paragraph by paragraph, using pictures and words together.
Guess a new word from the sentences around it, then check.
One Goal More shows that passing, listening and fair play belong with scoring.

lessons.title: Finding and organising information
objectives: Search for a short, suitable text about a game.
Read a mind map and pick out facts.
Keep personal information private while using a device.
lessons.intro: A screen can show more stories than one shelf of books. It can also show pages that are too hard, untrue or unkind. Knowing how to search, and when to stop, is part of reading.
lessons.notes:
### A simple search
To look for information, open the browser or learning app your teacher allows. Type a few clear words, such as rules of handball or how to pass in netball. Read the list of titles before you tap. Choose a page with short sentences and a named writer or a known organisation, such as a school site or a sports body.

Skim the headings. If the page is a long article for adults, go back and choose another. A useful page for you answers one question in language you can read aloud.

### Stay safe
Use the device with a teacher or a parent nearby. Do not type your full name, the name of your school, your photograph, your home area or a phone number into a search or a comment box. If a page asks you to pay, to download something, or to meet a stranger, close it and tell an adult. If the words are cruel or the pictures frighten you, leave the page.

### A mind map
A mind map is a drawing that organises ideas. The topic sits in the middle. Branches lead to groups of facts. A mind map about handball might have four branches:

- Players: team, captain, referee
- Equipment: ball, kit, whistle, field
- Rules: pass, do not hold the ball too long, listen for the whistle
- Qualities: fair play, practice, cheering kindly

You can read a mind map by starting at the centre and following one branch at a time. You can also make one after you read, to prove you remember the groups of ideas.

### Mimes and videos
A mime tells a story with the body and no words. If you watch a short video or a mime of a match, ask: Who is the referee? What feeling does the face show? What happens next? Answer from what you saw, not from a guess you cannot point to.

keyWords.meaning: a drawing with a topic in the middle and branches of related ideas
to look quickly at titles and headings to see what a text is about
a program used to open pages on the internet
acting out a meaning with the body and without spoken words

examples.problem: Which search is more useful for a Grade 4 reader: 'netball' or 'simple netball rules for children'?
steps: A single word brings many kinds of pages.
A phrase that names the topic and the level is easier to choose from.

examples.problem: A page asks you to type your school's name and your photograph. What should you do?
steps: Personal details are not needed for reading about a game.
An adult should know about the request.
examples.answer: Close the page and tell a teacher or parent. Do not type those details.

activity.title: Mind map of a favourite game
materials: A shared digital device if the teacher provides one
steps: With the teacher, search for one short text about a game using clear words.
Read the title and headings, then pick out four facts.
Draw a mind map with the game in the centre and branches for players, equipment, rules and qualities.
Explain your mind map to another group. If a page felt wrong or asked for private details, say so and leave it.

practice.question: What is a mind map?
practice.answer: A drawing with the topic in the middle and branches that group related facts.

practice.question: Name two pieces of information you should not type into a webpage.
practice.answer: Any two: your full name, your school's name, your photograph, your home area, a phone number.

practice.question: Why do you read headings before you read a whole page?
practice.answer: To see whether the page answers your question and is suitable for you.

practice.question: Name the four branches used on the handball mind map in this lesson.

summary: Search with clear words and choose a short, suitable page.
Do not share personal details online. Tell an adult about a worrying page.
A mind map groups facts so they are easy to remember and explain.

lessons.title: A poem, a puzzle and a reason to read
objectives: Read a poem aloud so that the feelings are clear.
Build simple crossword clues from a text.
Explain why digital reading is useful for learning.
lessons.intro: The same match can be a story or a poem. A poem asks you to hear the beats and the feelings. Read this one as if you were performing it for your team.
lessons.notes:
### Four Feelings on the Field
Before the whistle I am tight.
My hands are cold. My mouth is dry.
I hear the coach say, 'Breathe and pass.'
I lift my eyes and try.

The ball arrives. I do not freeze.
I throw it cleanly to the wing.
The crowd's loud shout rolls over us,
And hope feels sudden, bright and wide.

Then comes a miss. The ball rolls out.
My shoulders drop. I want to hide.
A teammate nods and taps my arm:
'Stay with us. Play. We still have time.'

The final whistle. We have won.
We clap the team that played so fair.
I walk off slowly, dusty, glad,
And proud of every pass we shared.

### Reading with feeling
Each stanza has its own feeling. The first is nervous. The second is hopeful. The third is disappointed, then encouraged. The fourth is glad and proud. Change your speed and your face to match. Do not race through a sad line in a cheerful shout.

You can do the same with a cartoon or a comic. Read the words in the speech balloons, then look at the face in the picture. If they disagree, trust the words and notice the joke or the mistake.

### A small crossword from the texts
A crossword uses clues. The answers are words from the poem or the story.

- The person who says 'Breathe and pass' (5 letters): coach
- Glad and pleased with the team (5 letters): proud
- The sound the crowd makes (5 letters): shout
- What the referee blows (7 letters): whistle

Making the clues yourself proves you understood the text.

### Why read on a screen
Digital books, poems and videos let you reread, listen and sometimes watch the story move. They help you learn a game even when the library shelf is small. They are useful only when you choose suitable pages, read them carefully and talk about what you found. Reading for information and enjoyment can continue long after this class if you keep the habit.

keyWords.meaning: a grouped set of lines in a poem, like a paragraph in a story
a hint that helps you find an answer
a story told in pictures with speech balloons
showing feeling clearly through the voice or face

examples.problem: Which feeling fits the third stanza, and which line supports your answer?
steps: Read the third stanza only.
Look for words about the body and the miss.
examples.answer: Disappointment. 'My shoulders drop. I want to hide.' The teammate then encourages the speaker.

examples.problem: Write a crossword clue for the word whistle, using the story One Goal More.
steps: Recall who uses a whistle.
Write a short clue that does not contain the word itself.
examples.answer: Example: The referee blows this to start and stop the match. (7 letters)

activity.title: Perform and puzzle
materials: A screen if you watch a short mime or cartoon
steps: In groups, give each stanza to one learner. Rehearse, then perform the poem so the feelings change.
If a video or mime is available, watch it and answer: Who acts? What feeling do you see? What happens last?
Create four crossword clues from the poem or the story. Swap with another group and solve theirs.
Tell the class one reason you would choose a digital poem or story again.

practice.question: Name the four feelings, in order, in the poem.
practice.answer: Nervous, hopeful, disappointed (then encouraged), glad and proud.

practice.question: What does the coach tell the speaker to do in the first stanza?
Give one reason to read poems or stories on a screen.
practice.answer: You can reread them, sometimes hear or watch them, and find texts even when few printed copies are available.

practice.question: What should you do if a digital story uses words or pictures that frighten you?
practice.answer: Leave the page and tell a teacher or parent.

summary: Change your voice to match the feeling of each stanza.
Crossword clues made from a text show that you understood it.
Digital reading helps learning when the texts are suitable and you read them with care.

quiz.question: In One Goal More, why did the other team score first?
options: The narrator held the ball too long
quiz.explanation: The narrator held the first pass too long and the other team took the ball.

quiz.question: What did pointing to the ear mean?
quiz.explanation: The story says the gesture meant listen.

quiz.question: The score was level means
options: both teams had the same score

quiz.question: What did the teams do when the match ended?
options: They left the ball on the road
quiz.explanation: They shook hands with each other.

quiz.question: Which search words are clearest for a young reader?
quiz.explanation: Clear words name the topic and the kind of page you need.

quiz.question: Where does the topic sit on a mind map?
options: Only at the bottom of the page
quiz.explanation: The topic is in the centre, with branches around it.

quiz.question: A page asks for your photograph and your school's name. You should
options: close the page and tell an adult
quiz.explanation: Do not share personal details. Tell a teacher or parent.

quiz.question: The third stanza of the poem mainly shows
options: a miss and disappointment, then encouragement
the start of a race in the rain
a silent empty field with no players
quiz.explanation: The ball rolls out, the shoulders drop, and a teammate says there is still time.

quiz.question: Why is it useful to read suitable texts on a screen?
quiz.answer: You can find, reread and sometimes watch or hear poems and stories, which supports learning and enjoyment.
quiz.explanation: Digital reading adds ways to meet texts when you choose them carefully.

quiz.question: Which habit makes digital reading worthwhile?
options: Choosing suitable texts and talking about what you learned
Typing your home details for fun
quiz.explanation: Careful choice and discussion turn screen time into learning.
